name: AI Literacy
purpose: This exam assesses whether candidates understand how generative AI works and its limitations, and can use it safely and effectively at work. It validates the common vocabulary every candidate needs, regardless of role.
guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates understand how generative AI works and its limitations, and can use it safely and effectively at work. It validates the common vocabulary every candidate needs, regardless of role.

**Objectives**

- Explain how LLMs generate responses and the resulting limitations: hallucinations, knowledge cutoffs, and context limits.
- Distinguish product formats suited to different tasks: chat, projects, custom assistants, agents, and APIs.
- Apply basic prompting habits that improve quality through clear instructions and context.
- Understand usage policies and data handling, and follow principles for handling sensitive information.
- Explain adoption value and risks from an organizational perspective.

### 2. Target candidates

- Office professionals, service planners, product managers, training specialists

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- No technical background is required. Coding, architecture design, and model training are out of scope.

### 3. Content domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Generative AI fundamentals | 20% |
| 2. Effective use | 25% |
| 3. Product formats and feature categories | 20% |
| 4. Responsible use and data | 15% |
| 5. Adoption value and organizational perspective | 20% |

**Domain 1: Generative AI fundamentals**

- Knowledge: Tokens, context windows, probabilistic generation, knowledge cutoffs, why hallucinations occur, reasoning (thinking) versus standard models, and multimodal input.
- Skills: Choose an appropriate large, medium, or lightweight model tier for task difficulty; identify situations where model output should not be accepted at face value.

**Domain 2: Effective use**

- Knowledge: Clear and specific instructions, examples, roles and background, output formats, and task decomposition.
- Skills: Turn vague requests into specific ones, provide context with files and images, and iteratively improve results.

**Domain 3: Product formats and feature categories**

- Knowledge: Differences between chat apps, projects (knowledge spaces), custom assistants (GPTs, Gems, project instructions; GPTs are scheduled for retirement and Gems are transitioning to skills), connectors, agent features, coding agents, and APIs.
- Skills: Select suitable product formats for repetitive work, document-based questions, and external app integrations.

**Domain 4: Responsible use and data**

- Knowledge: Prohibited-use categories shared by the three providers, differences in data retention and training use between consumer and enterprise plans, and the availability of administrative controls.
- Skills: Decide whether sensitive information may be entered; verify AI-generated content and its sources.

**Domain 5: Adoption value and organizational perspective**

- Knowledge: Subscription versus token-based billing, use-case selection criteria, and the purpose of the three providers' frontier safety frameworks.
- Skills: Prioritize use cases by high impact and low risk; propose metrics for measuring adoption outcomes.

questions.title: Knowledge cutoffs and questions about recent information
questions.prompt: A marketing employee asks an internal general-purpose AI chat tool, "Summarize the eligibility requirements in the government funding announcement published last week." The tool is configured to use only the model's own knowledge, without web search or file attachments. It confidently produces a plausible list of requirements. What is the **most appropriate** way to treat this answer?

options.text: The model provided specific requirements without hesitation, so assume the announcement was in its training data and use the answer as is.
Ask the same question in a new conversation; if the answers match, treat the information as accurate rather than fabricated.
The announcement may postdate the model's knowledge cutoff, so verify the original announcement or provide it and ask again.
A larger context window contains more recent information, so switch to a model with a larger context window and ask again.

questions.explanation:
Models are built from data available up to a particular point, so their reliable knowledge has a cutoff. Anthropic's model comparison table lists a separate "Reliable knowledge cutoff" for each model. When asked about later events, a model may invent plausible information (hallucinate). Check the original source directly, or provide it as context and ask the model to answer using only that material.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Specificity and confidence do not guarantee accuracy. Hallucinations are often fluent and confidently expressed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Comparing repeated runs can signal hallucination when answers disagree. Agreement between two answers does not verify facts occurring after the cutoff.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Recognizing the cutoff and verifying against a current source, or providing the source for a grounded answer, is appropriate.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: The context window is the working memory used to generate a response, separate from training data. Increasing it does not supply recent facts the model never learned.

Also note: Tools with web search or connectors can retrieve current information, but you should still open and verify their sources.

**References**: [Models overview › Compare models](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview) · [Context windows › How the context window works](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) · [Reduce hallucinations › Advanced techniques](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)

questions.title: Match reasoning effort to the task
questions.prompt:
Nuri Logistics uses one OpenAI reasoning model at the **highest reasoning effort** for two operations tasks.

- Task 1: Compare constraints across several departments each month to plan a warehouse relocation schedule. The team is satisfied with the quality.
- Task 2: Classify thousands of daily inquiry emails as "Shipping/Refund/Other." The team reports **slow processing and high costs**.

Reasoning models think internally before answering, and those tokens are billed as output tokens. Which adjustment **best reduces the problems in Task 2 while preserving the quality of Task 1**?

options.text: Reduce reasoning effort to the lowest level for both tasks to lower overall latency and cost at once.
Keep the current setting for Task 1, and disable reasoning or use the lowest level only for Task 2.
Switch both tasks to a higher-tier reasoning model to improve both planning quality and classification accuracy.
Move Task 1 to a fast, cheaper model and retain the current settings for Task 2 to preserve classification accuracy.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's reasoning documentation describes reasoning models as particularly strong at complex problem solving and multistep tasks. It recommends no reasoning for latency-sensitive tasks that gain little from reasoning, such as voice, quick lookups, and classification, and high reasoning for difficult work such as deep planning. The standard approach is therefore to set reasoning effort separately for each task. Reasoning tokens are not displayed but are billed as output tokens, so high reasoning on simple classification adds time and cost. The key evidence is [preserving Task 1 quality] and [Task 2 latency and cost complaints].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It helps Task 2 but also reduces reasoning for Task 1's cross-department constraint analysis, violating the quality requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: High reasoning for complex planning and no or minimal reasoning for simple classification satisfy both requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Task 2's complaint concerns speed and cost, not accuracy. Upgrading the model targets quality while leaving excessive reasoning for simple classification unchanged.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Matching reasoning to the task is the right idea, but the allocation is reversed. Reducing it for deep planning while retaining it for simple classification makes both problems worse.

Also note: Gemini's documentation follows the same principle, recommending low thinking for simple factual lookups and classification, and high thinking for complex work.

**References**: [Reasoning models › How reasoning works](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning) · [Gemini thinking › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: Check instructions from the perspective of a colleague without context
questions.prompt: A finance employee attaches quarterly results to Claude and writes only, "Organize this. Keep it brief." The result differs from expectations, leading to repeated requests. Under Claude's official prompting guidance, what should the employee **apply first** when revising the request?

options.text: State the purpose, audience, and desired output so that even a colleague without context could follow the instructions.
Repeatedly emphasize prohibitions such as "Never write at length!" using bold text and exclamation marks.
Shorten the request further so the model has more freedom to infer the intention from the attachment.
Remove the attachment and transcribe only key numbers to minimize the amount the model must read.

questions.explanation:
Claude's guidance recommends treating the model like a capable new employee with no context, and specifying the desired result and constraints. Its golden rule is that if a colleague with little context would be confused by the prompt, the model will be confused too. Explaining the motivation or reason behind instructions also helps the model understand the goal and respond appropriately.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Specifying purpose, audience, and format is central to being clear and direct. The colleague test fits this situation.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: For output formatting, the guide recommends saying what to do rather than what not to do, and explaining reasons instead of repeating emphasis. Without specifying the desired outcome, stronger prohibitions leave the underlying problem unsolved.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The guide says to explicitly request the level of output you want rather than expect the model to infer it. Increasing ambiguity does the opposite.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The original material supplies necessary context for the summary. Removing it reduces the information available as evidence.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Be clear and direct](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Add context to improve performance](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompting best practices › Control the format of responses](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Improve responses with examples and context
questions.prompt: Nuri Logistics uses Gemini to draft customer support replies. Many replies contain **generic advice inconsistent with company procedures**, and **format and tone vary between replies**. According to Google's prompt design strategies, choose **TWO** effective ways to address these problems.

options.text: Mix exemplary replies with different formats and structures so the model learns a range of styles.
Provide relevant background material, such as the company troubleshooting guide, and ask for answers based on it.
Include as many past exemplary replies as possible so that no category is omitted.
Include a few examples of the desired replies, keeping their structure and formatting consistent.
Leave the materials unchanged and add a forceful instruction: "You must answer only according to our company procedures."

questions.explanation:
Google's documentation shows that without context, a model offers generic troubleshooting information, while adding the relevant guide produces answers tailored to that material. It also recommends few-shot examples with consistent structure and formatting to prevent unwanted formats from appearing. The two clues are "generic advice" (missing context) and "inconsistent format and tone" (example consistency).

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Using examples is appropriate, but the documentation calls for consistent structure and formatting. Mixing formats can worsen the inconsistency.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Generic advice results from missing company-specific context; supplying relevant material directly addresses it.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: The documentation warns that too many examples can cause responses to overfit to them, and recommends experimenting to find the right number.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A few consistently structured examples can correct variations in format and tone.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Stronger wording does not tell the model what the company procedures are, so generic advice remains. Gemini 3 guidance also recommends clear, concise goals and avoiding unnecessarily coercive language.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Add context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Zero-shot vs few-shot prompts](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Gemini 3 › Core prompting principles](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

questions.title: Request a proposal draft from meeting notes
questions.prompt: A Nuri Logistics salesperson uses Gemini in a company-approved work account to draft proposals from client meeting notes. Previously, they pasted the notes and asked only, "Organize this into a proposal." The output was **a generic introduction that could suit any client** and **did not follow the company proposal structure**. Company rules prohibit **entering client contacts' names or contact details into AI**. According to Google's prompt design strategies, which request is **most appropriate** this time?

options.text: Remove contact information from the notes but leave the request unchanged, regenerating until the result matches the company structure.
Omit the notes, summarize the client industry and interests in two or three lines, and specify the proposal purpose, outline, length, and tone in detail.
Include the original notes, including contact details, and use delimiters to specify the proposal purpose, audience, outline, and length in detail.
Include notes with contact information removed, state the proposal purpose, audience, outline, and length, and separate the notes from instructions with delimiters.

questions.explanation:
Google's documentation shows that providing the information needed for the task (adding context) produces specific answers grounded in that material instead of generic advice. It also explains that instructions can specify formats such as lists, tables, and outlines. Gemini 3 guidance recommends delimiters, such as tags or Markdown, to separate instructions, context, and tasks. The clues are [content that could suit any client] (missing context) and [different company structure] (unspecified format). The [exclude contact information] rule constrains which context may be provided.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Iterative improvement means changing the prompt itself: rephrasing, trying a similar task, or rearranging content. Regenerating without revising the request leaves the missing format specification unresolved.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: The format improves, but details from this meeting are missing, so the result remains generic. Concerns about sensitive information do not justify removing necessary context as well.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Context, format, and delimiters are present, but including client names and contact details violates company policy. Contact details are not necessary context for the proposal either.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Filtered notes provide compliant context, explicit purpose, audience, and structure guide the result, and separating notes from instructions addresses both problems.

Also note: If the company has a proposal template, one or two consistently structured examples can further help match the format.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Add context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Clear and specific instructions › Response format](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Gemini 3 › Structured prompting examples](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Prompt iteration strategies](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

questions.title: A product feature for ongoing teamwork
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Design Studio uses a ChatGPT workspace. During a three-month brand renewal project, it wants to:

- Keep related conversations together and continue work over time
- Avoid re-uploading brand guidelines and work instructions every time
- Work **together with teammates** in the same context

Which feature best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a brand-renewal project, upload the guidelines and instructions, and invite teammates to chat in the same project.
Have each teammate create an individual project, upload the same guidelines and instructions, and collect their own related conversations there.
Create and share a brand-renewal project, but attach the guidelines to a conversation every time work begins.
Keep the guidelines in the company drive and connect it through Connected apps, then share an instruction document with all teammates.

questions.explanation:
ChatGPT Projects bring related conversations, files, and instructions together to maintain context for ongoing work. Project instructions apply only within the project and take precedence over global custom instructions. Projects can be shared with individuals, groups, or through a link for collaboration.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It collects conversations in one project, requires uploading files and instructions only once, and lets teammates work in the same project, satisfying all three requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It collects conversations and avoids repeated uploads, but separate personal projects do not let teammates collaborate in the same context.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It collects conversations and supports team sharing, but repeatedly attaching the guidelines violates the requirement to avoid re-uploading.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Teammates can access the same materials without re-uploading, but it does not collect related conversations in one place for continued work, so it fails the first requirement.

Claude Projects, with project knowledge and instructions, similarly enable context reuse. OpenAI help describes plans to retire custom GPTs, which should be considered when designing new workflows.

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Add context to guide responses](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Projects in ChatGPT › Share a project](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Creating and editing GPTs › Overview](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8554397-creating-and-editing-gpts) · [How can I create and manage projects? › Adding content to project knowledge](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177)

questions.title: Match product formats to situations
questions.prompt:
Choose the most suitable product format on the right for each work situation on the left. One option is unused.

| Work situation | Product format |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Polish the wording of one email to a business partner, then finish | a. Regular chat |
| 2. Collect conversations, files, and instructions for a quarter-long new product initiative and use them with teammates | b. Project |
| 3. Find and reference current documents from the company drive and messenger during a conversation | c. Connector (external service integration) |
| 4. A development team embeds AI in its customer-facing app and controls its behavior precisely | d. API |
| 5. Delegate a long-running, multistep task and receive the result asynchronously | e. Managed agent |
| | f. Dedicated image generation tool |

options.text: Regular chat
Project
Connector (external service integration)
API
Managed agent
Dedicated image generation tool

items.text: Polish the wording of one email to a business partner, then finish
Collect conversations, files, and instructions for a quarter-long new product initiative and use them with teammates
Find and reference current documents from the company drive and messenger during a conversation
A development team embeds AI in its customer-facing app and controls its behavior precisely
Delegate a long-running, multistep task and receive the result asynchronously

questions.explanation:
Product formats are easier to select by asking how long the work lasts, who shares it, whether external data is needed, whether the feature is being built into a product, and how long and autonomously it runs.

| Item | Rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1 → a | Regular chat is sufficient for a one-off task that does not need retained context. |
| 2 → b | Projects collect and share related conversations, files, and instructions. |
| 3 → c | Connectors, such as ChatGPT Connected apps, search and reference external drive or messenger information during a conversation. |
| 4 → d | Claude documentation describes the Messages API as direct model access with fine-grained control. Embedding a feature into a product is development work. |
| 5 → e | Claude Managed Agents is an agent runtime on managed infrastructure, described as suitable for long-running and asynchronous tasks. |
| f | Image generation is not a core requirement in any of the situations, so this option is unused. |

**References**: [Projects in ChatGPT › Overview](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt) · [Connected apps in ChatGPT › Understand app capabilities](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11487775-connected-apps-in-chatgpt) · [Intro to Claude › Develop with Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/intro)

questions.title: Assess work material entered into a personal plan
questions.prompt: An employee realizes that they have spent several weeks revising internal report drafts in a personal Claude Pro consumer account **with model improvement enabled**. Company policy permits work material **only in company-managed plans**. According to Anthropic's privacy guidance, which judgment is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Delete all previous conversations. Deletion also removes the content from already-trained models, so nothing else is necessary.
Use only incognito conversations going forward. Since these are not used for model improvement, continuing with a personal plan is acceptable.
Disable the setting and move work material to the company plan. Data already incorporated into training cannot be reversed.
Only disable the setting. This retroactively removes past conversations from all training data, so it is sufficient.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic's consumer-plan guidance says that enabling model improvement can retain newly started or continued conversations in a de-identified training pipeline for up to five years. Disabling it prevents previous and new conversations from being used for future training. However, it does not remove data from training already underway or from trained models. The appropriate judgment recognizes the irreversible portion, prevents further exposure, and moves work material to a company-managed plan. The key facts are [past use with the setting enabled] and [work material allowed only in company-managed plans].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Deleted conversations are excluded from future training but are not removed from already-trained models. Deleted conversations disappear from history immediately and from the backend within 30 days.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Incognito conversations are indeed excluded from model improvement, but using a personal plan for work material still violates company policy.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It accurately recognizes the setting's effects and limitations and takes follow-up action consistent with organizational policy.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Disabling the setting affects future training, not retroactive removal of data already incorporated into training.

**References**: [How long do you store my data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data)

questions.title: Criteria for choosing initial adoption use cases
questions.prompt: A strategy team is choosing use cases for substantial investment during the first year of company-wide AI adoption. There are dozens of candidates and a limited budget. According to OpenAI's enterprise AI investment guidance, choose **TWO appropriate** screening criteria.

options.text: Does the work recur at meaningful scale, with a clearly accountable team?
Is it work performed by the team with the highest credit or message usage, so its value can be considered proven?
Can it start immediately by postponing security, legal, and IT review until scaling?
Can quality, risk, and business value be measured, with a "good enough" standard defined before testing?
Is it a one-off event with strong executive interest and significant publicity potential if successful?

questions.explanation:
OpenAI identifies promising workflows as recurring at meaningful scale, having a clear owner, and offering measurable quality, risk, and business value. It also stresses defining "good enough" before testing and establishing governance, including required context, tools, and approval paths, before scaling.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Recurring scale and clear ownership are explicit selection criteria.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Usage signals demand, not proof of value. High-usage work merits investigation, but usage alone does not justify investment.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: OpenAI's enterprise scaling guidance says organizations that involved security, legal, compliance, and IT as early design partners had fewer reversals later. Postponing governance takes the opposite approach.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Measurability and predefined quality standards are prerequisites for demonstrating impact and deciding whether to scale.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: One-off tasks lack recurring scale, making cumulative returns difficult. Executive attention and publicity are not the document's screening criteria.

**References**: [How to manage AI investments in the agentic era](https://openai.com/index/managing-ai-investments-in-agentic-era/) · [How enterprises are scaling AI](https://openai.com/business/guides-and-resources/how-enterprises-are-scaling-ai/)

questions.title: Measure the impact of adoption
questions.prompt: Nuri Logistics has piloted an AI tool in customer support for three months. Management requests **a performance report that supports a decision on expansion**. The support manager is choosing how to measure results. According to official OpenAI and Anthropic guidance, which method is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Report steadily rising logins and conversation counts during the pilot as the main evidence of successful adoption.
Compare the cost per resolved case meeting predefined quality standards, including human review, against the pre-pilot baseline.
Calculate monthly fee savings from using the model with the lowest unit price for the same work, and report those savings.
Survey employee satisfaction after the pilot, then set the success threshold after reviewing the response distribution.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI's AI investment guidance says usage and unit price alone do not reveal value. It recommends cost per accepted outcome, such as a resolved support inquiry, alongside business value such as turnaround time and capacity gained. Costs include retries and human review. Anthropic likewise recommends specific, measurable success criteria defined in advance, with examples expressed as improvement over an existing baseline. The key clue is the report's purpose: [deciding whether to expand].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Usage signals demand and adoption, not proof of value. More usage says nothing about output quality or cost effectiveness.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It includes predefined quality standards, measurement per accepted outcome (resolved case), total costs including human review, and comparison with the pre-pilot baseline.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: A cheaper model may cost more overall if retries and rework increase. Comparing usage fees is one aspect of cost optimization, not an adoption-impact measure.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: User feedback can be useful, but setting standards after seeing results prevents objective assessment. The documents recommend defining criteria before testing.

**References**: [How to manage AI investments in the agentic era](https://openai.com/index/managing-ai-investments-in-agentic-era/) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Define your success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: What is a token?
questions.prompt: After pasting a 20-page report and requesting a summary, an employee sees "Input: 12,000 tokens / Output: 800 tokens" in an internal AI tool's usage screen. What is the **most appropriate** meaning of a token?

options.text: The number of documents used to train the model; a higher value means more recent training material.
A small piece of text processed by the model, used to measure input and output length.
The number of messages a user may send daily, used to measure usage limits.
Exactly one word in a sentence, so token count equals word count.

questions.explanation:
Generative AI models divide text into pieces called tokens rather than processing characters as-is. Google describes a token as possibly one character, one word, or part of a longer word; in English, 100 tokens correspond to roughly 60–80 words. Both input (questions and supplied material) and output (answers) are counted in tokens. Models have limits on tokens processed at once, and usage-based prices can depend on token counts.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Tokens measure the length of text currently processed, not the size of training data.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It correctly defines tokens as pieces of text measuring input and output volume.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Services may impose message-count limits, but these are usage policies, not the definition of tokens.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Tokens and words do not correspond one-to-one. Long words may split into several tokens; short words or symbols may count as one.

Also note: Inputs such as images and audio are also converted into tokens for processing.

**References**: [Understand and count tokens (Gemini API)](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tokens)

questions.title: Why early instructions are missed in long conversations
questions.prompt: A logistics-planning employee has spent over three hours refining a report in one chat while adding materials. The first instruction was "Refer to clients only as Company A and Company B," but recent answers show real client names. There is no outage notice. What is the **most likely cause**?

options.text: The model continually retrains on the conversation, so later content overwrote the initial rule.
Longer conversations move the knowledge cutoff backward, leaving the model unaware of the initial rule.
Reasoning effort automatically decreases over time, causing earlier instructions to be skipped.
The amount available for reference is limited, so earlier content has fallen out of context or received less attention.

questions.explanation:
The context window is the model's working memory for producing an answer, separate from training data. Anthropic explains that earlier messages and responses accumulate and are included in subsequent inputs, and accuracy and recall can deteriorate as token counts grow. - **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Conversation input enters working context; it does not immediately retrain the model itself.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: The knowledge cutoff concerns training-material dates and does not change with conversation length.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Reasoning effort does not automatically decline with elapsed time. It depends on the model and configuration.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Context limits and reduced accuracy on long inputs explain missing early instructions.

Also note: Summarize essential rules and paste them at the beginning of a fresh conversation.

questions.title: Revise one part while preserving what works
questions.prompt: An HR employee likes four paragraphs of an AI-generated five-paragraph notice, but the third sounds too stiff. Following the principle of directly and specifically requesting the desired result, what should the next request do?

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: The target and degree of softness are unclear, so other paragraphs may change.

questions.title: Choose effective examples
questions.prompt: A support team will include examples in prompts classifying inquiries as Shipping, Refund, Account, and similar categories. According to Claude guidance on effective examples, choose **TWO** practices.

Polish one typical case and leave the model to generalize all others.
Cover diverse types, including ambiguous inquiries combining shipping and refunds.
Simplify real inquiries into easy fictional scenarios for examples.
Use only easy representative cases and exclude confusing boundary cases.

questions.explanation:
Claude says effective examples must be relevant to real use and diverse enough to cover unexpected cases without teaching unintended patterns. In classification, ambiguous boundary cases help communicate the decision rule.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Realistic inquiries satisfy relevance.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: One case may teach superficial features as rules and lacks diversity.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Varied examples, including boundary cases, clarify classification criteria.

questions.title: Ask for interpretation of an attached chart
questions.prompt: A finance employee uploads a monthly-sales chart screenshot to Gemini and asks only "Analyze this chart." The answer merely reads axis names and values. The employee wants **interpretation beyond listing numbers**. Which next request is **most appropriate**?

Provide a clear image and ask which intervals changed most and what possible causes might explain them.
Crop to a small image of one interval so the model focuses only there.
Transcribe every value and omit the image to prevent reading errors.

questions.explanation:

- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Clear input and specific questions directly target interpretation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Cropping removes axes, legends, and comparison context, making trends harder to interpret. Scope is not the underlying issue.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Transcribing all values adds effort with little benefit when the image is already available, while the question remains vague.

questions.title: Sequence work from attachments to a proposal draft
questions.prompt:
A salesperson wants a proposal draft based on a client-interview file. Instead of one request, they will use four stages, **passing each result as input to the next**. Put these steps in order.

- (1) Request a proposal using the verified summary, specifying purpose, audience, and length.
- (2) Review the draft and request revisions with specific feedback.
- (3) Attach the interview file and request a summary of key requirements.
- (4) Check the summary against the interview and request corrections.

items.text: Request a proposal using the verified summary, specifying purpose, audience, and length.
Review the draft and request revisions with specific feedback.
Attach the interview file and request a summary of key requirements.
Check the summary against the interview and request corrections.

questions.explanation:
Google describes decomposing complex work so each output becomes the next input, and refining prompts based on results. Because later stages rely on earlier artifacts, verification checkpoints prevent errors propagating.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) Attach and summarize | None; supplies source material for all later stages. | Provide context. |
| 2 | (4) Verify and correct | A summary is needed for comparison. | Catch errors before drafting. |
| 3 | (1) Draft from verified summary | Uses corrected summary as input. | Chain outputs into inputs. |
| 4 | (2) Revise from feedback | A draft is needed to identify changes. | Iterative improvement. |

questions.title: Use purpose to resolve conflicting requirements
questions.prompt: An employee asks AI to summarize every contract condition within one page. The model arbitrarily omits some items. The employee adds, "This summary is for an approver to assess risky clauses." According to Claude guidance, what is the **most appropriate value** of stating this purpose?

options.text: The model recognizes importance and chooses more careful words, improving prose quality.
It thinks longer, eliminating factual errors in the summary.
It gains a basis for prioritizing between conflicting conditions.
It understands the use, allowing human review to be skipped.

questions.explanation:
Claude says explaining the reason behind instructions improves goal understanding and generalization. Here completeness conflicts with a one-page limit. Knowing the risk-assessment purpose gives the model criteria for retaining or compressing items. The clue is [two conflicting conditions].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Merely conveying importance does not establish better prose; concrete decision criteria are needed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Purpose does not determine reasoning time or eliminate factual errors.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Purpose supplies a basis for prioritization.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Understanding the use does not remove the need to compare the summary with the original.

questions.title: Combine long material and instructions in one message
questions.prompt: A legal employee will paste three very long contracts into Claude and request a comparison of termination conditions only. Mixed instructions and material may obscure boundaries. Which message structure is **most appropriate**?

options.text: Place contracts first, each grouped with a title or tags, and separate the instructions at the end.
Combine instructions and contracts into one paragraph and rely on contextual inference.
Insert the instruction repeatedly between contract passages.
Merge all contracts into one long text and mix instructions into its first paragraph.

questions.explanation:
Claude recommends long documents near the top, questions/instructions at the end, and tags distinguishing documents from instructions. Gemini 3 guidance likewise recommends tags or headings. The clues are [very long text] and [confusion between evidence and instructions].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It satisfies both clear separation and question-after-material ordering.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Without boundaries, source text may be mistaken for instructions or instruction scope may be lost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Scattered instructions interrupt document flow and blur boundaries further.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Merging contracts loses attribution of conditions and buries the instruction, undermining comparison.

questions.title: Explain unfamiliar internal terminology
questions.prompt: Nuri Logistics asks AI to summarize reports containing internal terms such as "dawn call" and "hub cutoff," leading to odd summaries. These terms **do not appear in public material**. Choose **TWO** ways to help the model understand them.

Do not explain meanings; manually fix incorrect summaries afterward.
Translate the entire request into English because unfamiliar terms cause errors.
Attach relevant manual passages using the terms and request answers grounded in them.
Add "Interpret internal terms appropriately from context" without other information.

questions.explanation:
Google recommends relevant references and guides for specific rather than generic answers. Claude recommends explaining necessary background as to a new employee without context. Nonpublic terms are unlikely to have been learned, so supply definitions or authentic usage material.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: A glossary directly and concisely supplies necessary context.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Manual cleanup repeats the work and leaves the missing-understanding cause unresolved.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Changing language does not provide unknown meanings.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Real usage material provides both meaning and application.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: An instruction without information invites guesswork to fill gaps.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Add context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompting best practices › Be clear and direct](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Create a reusable team prompt
questions.prompt: A support team requests the same weekly inquiry-summary structure every week. Members write new prompts each time, so **format and quality vary by person**. The lead wants less variation and **a method anyone can use immediately**. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Share the best member’s prompt in chat and allow unrestricted adaptation.
Share a template with fixed purpose, format, and constraints and marked slots for dates and source material.
Save one excellent output and request only "Make it like this" thereafter.
Standardize on one generic line: "Summarize weekly inquiries."

questions.explanation:
OpenAI distinguishes fixed application rules in developer messages from variable user input, comparing them to function definitions and arguments. Applied to everyday work, fix purpose, format, and constraints in a template and fill only changing material. Consistent requests reduce output variation and make reuse easy.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Sharing a good prompt helps, but undefined editable versus fixed parts permit renewed variation.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Separating fixed and variable portions provides consistency and usability.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: One output does not reveal the conditions that produced it, making quality hard to reproduce for different material.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: A generic line is reusable but omits the format and constraints, leaving variation unresolved.

**References**: [Prompt engineering › Message roles and instruction following](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering)

questions.title: Describe desired behavior instead of prohibitions
questions.prompt: An employee writes "Do not use jargon. Do not use difficult words. Do not write at length," but the answer still has difficult vocabulary and long paragraphs. Which revision best follows Claude guidance?

options.text: Expand the prohibitions into more than ten detailed items.
Repeat the same prohibitions again at both ends of the request.
Rephrase them politely as "Please avoid..."
Specify "Use words a middle-school student understands, with at most three sentences per paragraph."

questions.explanation:
Claude says specifying what to do works better than saying only what not to do. For example, asking for flowing prose is better than "Do not use Markdown." Prohibitions alone do not describe the desired result; specify concrete target vocabulary and length.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Repetition extends the same unsuccessful method.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Politeness changes wording but not the prohibition-only structure.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Positive, concrete vocabulary and length requirements directly define the goal.

Create a link allowing anyone holding it to enter the project.
Send files separately and have colleagues build their own projects.

questions.title: How memory is separated by project
questions.prompt: A planning employee uses separate Claude projects for a confidential acquisition review and routine reports. They worry that acquisition discussions will **enter other projects through memory**. According to Claude help, which judgment is most appropriate?

options.text: Project memory is public organization-wide, so confidential reviews should occur outside projects.

Each project has separate memory and does not use other projects’ memory, so use a dedicated review project.

questions.title: What Connected apps can do

questions.title: Connections versus uploads for current data
questions.prompt: A sales team drafts quotes with AI using a shared-drive price list updated almost daily. It wants **today’s prices without an owner uploading files**. Which approach best fits?

Connect the team drive and have the model retrieve the current sheet whenever drafting a quote.
Tell the model today’s date and ask it to recall prices for that date.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The copy stays outdated, risking stale quotes and requiring manual announcements.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Reading current source material follows updates without uploads.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The model has not learned internal prices; a date cannot supply unknown data and may encourage fabricated figures.

questions.title: What are agent capabilities?
questions.prompt: An operations employee must explain how an AI agent differs from regular chat. Which description is most appropriate?

options.text: A quick-response mode optimized to give one answer per question.
A capability that accepts a goal, plans stages, and uses tools to carry out multiple steps.
A dedicated model pretrained on every company document to answer any question immediately.
A setting applying the user’s tone and format rules consistently to every answer.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Lightweight models or reduced reasoning optimize speed; agents emphasize multistep execution.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Goal-directed, tool-supported sequences define agent behavior.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Training on documents is a separate development task, not the definition of agents.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Consistent tone and format belong to custom instructions or assistants.

questions.title: Where humans should approve an agent’s work
questions.prompt: An administration team plans to delegate: "Email three workshop venues for quotes, then pay the deposit at the cheapest one." The agent can browse, write email, and pay. Where should **human confirmation** occur?

Review one report after all work finishes and respond to any problems then.
Write careful initial instructions and let the agent complete everything autonomously.

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Reads and searches are lower-risk; approving everything removes delegation benefits.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Post-review helps assess quality but cannot readily undo sent mail or payments.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Good instructions cannot rule out unexpected judgments; irreversible actions still require approval.

questions.title: What does a coding agent do?

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Writing and customer support are ordinary chat or custom-assistant use cases.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Purchasing and installing servers is infrastructure operations, not a coding agent’s role.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Code reading, editing, and command execution support staged development work.

questions.title: Pilot an AI assistant without developers
questions.prompt: A sales team wants to test a proposal-drafting assistant **within four weeks without development staff**. It already uses a company AI chat app. Anthropic’s API onboarding involves SDK setup and API-key security. Which starting approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Hire a developer to build a dedicated API interface, then test after completion.
Have sales staff obtain API keys and write a model-calling program.
Put instructions and references into the existing chat app’s project or custom assistant and test it.
Collect past proposals and train a new sales-specific model.

questions.explanation:
APIs assume development work such as SDK configuration, secure key handling, and model calls. For a short pilot without developers, configuring an existing project or assistant is quicker and lighter. Once value is demonstrated, API integration can be considered. The decisive constraints are [no development staff] and [four weeks].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Hiring and development delay testing and spend before value is established.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Coding and key management impose substantial work on a nondevelopment team within four weeks.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Existing tools can test value with instructions and references alone.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Training is a separate large effort; instructions and references are sufficient to begin this pilot.

**References**: [Intro to Claude › Recommended path for new developers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/intro) · [Use Gems in Gemini Apps](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/15146780)

questions.title: Why use an API?
questions.prompt: A strategy employee asks why developers use APIs instead of chat apps. Choose **TWO valid reasons**.

options.text: To let programs automatically call the model within company products or business systems.
Because API conversations automatically retrain the model into a company-specific version.
To control model selection, system instructions, and invocation behavior precisely.
Because API access eliminates hallucinations by making models more accurate.
Because API models automatically know information after their cutoff without configuration.

questions.explanation:
An API gives developers direct model access through code. Anthropic describes Messages API as direct prompting with fine-grained control and model selection according to capability and cost. APIs suit embedding AI in products or controlling invocation behavior.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Programmatic model calls embed AI into products and workflows.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Calls do not automatically retrain models; customization requires separate development.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Code can control model choice, system prompts, and features.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The generation process remains the same and hallucinations remain possible; important API output also requires verification.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The cutoff is unchanged; current information needs retrieval or supplied material.

**References**: [Intro to Claude › Develop with Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/intro)

questions.title: A Google product for source-based questions
questions.prompt: A legal team using Gemini wants to collect documents for one lawsuit and **ask questions grounded in them**, create **quizzes or audio overviews**, and **separate cases**. Which option best fits?

options.text: Create one Gem per case and summarize document essentials into its instructions.
Create a Gemini Notebook for each case, add documents, and ask questions there.
Paste every case’s documents into one general Gemini conversation.
Read each document aloud to Gemini Live and ask questions.

questions.explanation:
Gemini Notebook groups project sources into notebooks and uses them for summaries and Q&A in Chat. Studio creates audio/video overviews, flashcards, quizzes, and reports. Notebooks are independent and cannot access one another's information, supporting case separation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Gems customize behavior through instructions and optional files, rather than centering source collections and learning artifacts.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It satisfies case separation, source-based questions, and learning artifacts.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Mixing cases breaks separation and may exceed context limits.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Gemini Live is for spoken conversation, not source management and artifact creation.

Also note: Notebook answers are AI-generated and should be checked against originals before legal judgments.

**References**: [Create a notebook in Gemini Notebook](https://support.google.com/notebooklm/answer/16206563) · [Use Gems in Gemini Apps](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/15146780)

questions.title: Evaluate statements about product formats
questions.prompt:
Mark each statement **Yes if correct, No if incorrect** according to official help.

1. Gems created in Gemini can be shared with others.
2. Gemini Notebook can combine sources from multiple notebooks to answer one question.
3. Agents autonomously complete irreversible actions, so separate human checkpoints are unnecessary.
4. Claude projects are available only on paid plans, not free plans.

items.text: Gems created in Gemini can be shared with others.

questions.title: Personal versus team-plan sharing and administration
questions.prompt: Six product-team members want to **share one Claude project** containing common files and instructions, with **central administration of accounts and costs**. Each currently has a personal subscription. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Each member creates a personal project and manually keeps identical files.
Create the project in one personal account and share its login credentials.
Move to Team, share the project within the organization, and let an administrator manage members.
Create six free accounts and exchange files between separate projects.

questions.explanation:
Claude Team centralizes access and billing and offers SSO and role-based permissions. Team and Enterprise projects can remain private or be shared with the organization, with use-only or edit roles. Personal subscriptions are account-specific rather than a centrally managed shared-project structure.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: Separate copies are not one project, can diverge, and lack central administration.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates constraints)**: Shared credentials obscure who did what and do not provide the required account management.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It combines project sharing with centralized accounts and billing.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: More free accounts only expand project counts, not sharing or administration.

**References**: [What is the Team plan?](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9266767-what-is-the-team-plan) · [How can I create and manage projects? › Sharing projects](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9519177)

questions.title: Choose a feature for recurring monthly reports
questions.prompt: On the first business day each month, an operations team opens last month’s order sheet in a shared drive, summarizes by region, and creates a report. It wants AI to **carry out the connected steps through document creation**, with **human review before submission**. Both chat and agent features are available. What is best?

options.text: Delegate sheet access through report creation to an agent, then have a person review the finished document.
Copy sheet data into chat and separately request each summary and document stage.
Ask general chat for last month’s regional orders and let it answer from known figures.
Create a custom assistant containing only tone and document-template rules.

questions.explanation:
Regular chat typically requires people to move data and request each stage. Agents accept goals and connect the necessary steps, fitting recurring multistage report work. Humans should still review the final artifact. The decisive requirements are [delegating through document creation] and [human review].

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It delegates the linked stages while retaining final review.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Suitable for a one-off task, but retains monthly copying and repeated requests.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The model does not know internal order figures and may invent them without supplied data.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Saved tone/template rules do not themselves open sheets and execute linked stages.

**References**: [Intro to Claude › Develop with Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/intro) · [Connected apps in ChatGPT › Understand app capabilities](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11487775-connected-apps-in-chatgpt)

questions.title: Uses prohibited by all three providers
questions.prompt: A new-hire training guide needs an example of a use prohibited by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. Which candidate should be presented as **prohibited by all three**?

options.text: Draft a farewell message using a departing colleague’s real name.
Simplify an internal training document containing legal terminology for new hires.
Draft an email impersonating a business partner’s employee to request a payment-account change.
Compare public prices and user reviews of an overseas competitor’s product.

questions.explanation:
Despite different wording, all three policies prohibit deception such as fraud, scams, and impersonation. Anthropic groups fraud and phishing under Fraudulent, Abusive, or Predatory Practices; OpenAI prohibits fraud, scams, and impersonation; Google prohibits misleading activities including scams and impersonation. The payment-account impersonation email directly fits these categories.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Naming a real person is not impersonating them. The prohibition concerns deceptive identity claims.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Legal subject matter itself is not prohibited; deceptive or harmful purposes are the concern here.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It assists impersonation and payment fraud, prohibited by all three.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Summarizing public information is ordinary work, not prohibited by these policies.

Also note: High-risk legal, medical, or financial uses may have extra conditions; Anthropic, for example, requires qualified review and AI-use disclosure when recommendations inform actual decisions.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy › Do Not Engage in Fraudulent, Abusive, or Predatory Practices](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) · [OpenAI Usage policies › Empower People](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/) · [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy › Misinformation, misrepresentation, or misleading activities](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy)

questions.title: Information to prohibit in AI inputs
questions.prompt: Hanbit Accounting’s security team is preparing a prohibited-input list, recognizing that input is transmitted to a service and may be retained. Choose **TWO information types** that belong on it.

options.text: A customer interview already published on the company’s official blog.
Configuration notes containing internal-system login credentials and access keys.
A routine work log with no client or contract information.
A draft contract containing nonpublic prices and delivery terms under negotiation.
A collection of publicly accessible product-review posts.

questions.explanation:
Inputs are transmitted and retained for some period. For example, Anthropic consumer conversations may take up to 30 days to disappear from the backend after deletion, and OpenAI says API inputs/outputs may be retained up to 30 days. Credentials and nonpublic business information are difficult to recover once exposed and should be prohibited. The test is public status and potential harm, not whether names appear.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Customer names may appear, but the company has already published them.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Exposed login credentials and keys can enable system compromise.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Internal status alone does not require prohibition; routine nonsensitive logs pose limited risk.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Negotiated prices and terms are confidential business information.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Publicly available posts are not nonpublic information.

**References**: [How long do you store my data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data) · [Enterprise privacy at OpenAI](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)

questions.title: Training-use defaults in team and personal plans
questions.prompt: Hanbit Accounting has adopted Claude Team for all employees. One asks, "I had to disable model improvement in my personal Pro account. Must everyone do that on Team too?" According to Anthropic privacy guidance, which explanation is most appropriate?

options.text: Inputs and outputs are not used for training by default, but conversations submitted as feedback may be exceptions.
It works like personal plans; each employee must disable model improvement to exclude their chats.
Inputs and outputs train models by default until the administrator requests exclusion.
Inputs and outputs never train models, including conversations submitted as feedback.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic commercial products—Team, Enterprise, and API—do not use inputs and outputs for training by default. Consumer Free, Pro, and Max plans instead offer individual model-improvement choices. In commercial products, feedback such as thumbs-up/down or explicit participation can make the related conversation available for improvement. Team/Enterprise owners can disable feedback submission in organization settings.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It accurately states the default and feedback exception.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Individual model-improvement settings describe consumer plans; Team has a different default.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: The default is reversed; commercial exclusion does not require advance application.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Feedback conversations may be used, so absolute exclusion is incorrect.

Also note: This distinction supports handling work material only in company-managed plans.

**References**: [Is my data used for model training? (commercial products)](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training) · [Is my data used for model training? (consumer plans)](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023580-is-my-data-used-for-model-training)

questions.title: Handle personal information visible in screenshots
questions.prompt: A Nuri Logistics IT employee wants AI help with an order-management error screenshot. Besides the error, the right side shows **customer names, mobile numbers, and delivery addresses**. Company rules prohibit customer identifiers in AI tools. Which approach meets the rule while obtaining help?

options.text: Upload unchanged because images are pictures, not textual input.
Upload the full screenshot and instruct the model to ignore customer information.
Upload it, receive the answer, then ask the model to delete the image.
Crop to the error or mask customer-information areas before uploading.

questions.explanation:
Multimodal models read image text, so names and numbers in screenshots are input information just like typed text. Apply the necessary-information-only principle to attachments before transmission. The error area is sufficient here. The clues are [the accompanying order list] and [the identifier prohibition].

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Image text is readable and therefore transmitted information.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: An ignore instruction cannot undo transmission; filter beforehand.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Uploading already violates the rule. On consumer services, conversation data may enter training before deletion.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Cropping or masking preserves useful error context while satisfying policy.

**References**: [How long do you store my data?](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023548-how-long-do-you-store-my-data)

questions.title: Google Workspace Gemini administrator controls
questions.prompt: An employee at Hanbit Accounting asks the IT administrator whether the company can control Gemini use or whether everyone manages it individually. According to Workspace guidance, which answer is most appropriate?

options.text: There are no admin controls; individuals choose usage and retention.
Administrators can enable/disable Gemini and its Workspace-app features and set conversation retention.
Administrators can set retention but cannot disable Gemini because it is a core service.
Admin settings affect only Gemini, not features within Docs or Gmail.

questions.explanation:
Workspace administrators can disable Gemini, decide whether conversations are saved, and select automatic deletion after 3, 18, or 36 months. In supported editions they can control Gemini features and side panels in Gmail, Drive, Docs, Meet, and Chat, and restrict grounding data sources. The key knowledge is that organizational controls exist.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Administration controls usage and retention.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It accurately covers app-level controls, embedded features, and retention.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Gemini is a core service enabled by default, but administrators can disable it.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Embedded Workspace Gemini features can also be controlled separately.

**References**: [Generative AI in Google Workspace Privacy Hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/generative-ai/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub)

questions.title: Checking source links supplied by AI
questions.prompt: An operations employee uses ChatGPT search to find the size of the domestic logistics market. The answer contains a figure and two source links, and the employee plans to use it in a monthly report. According to the help guidance, which verification is most appropriate?

options.text: Because links mean ChatGPT verified the evidence, check only that there are at least two sources.
Open the links to confirm the pages load, then cite the figure because a source exists.
Open the source page and check that it actually supports the figure and verify its publication date.
Check whether the site is a well-known news outlet or public agency, then cite the figure unchanged.

questions.explanation:
ChatGPT search guidance warns that search results and citations can be incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. It recommends opening cited sources to check whether they support the claim and to verify the publication or update date. The important context is that the figure will be used in a report.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect)**: A link is not proof that the evidence was verified. The linked page may not support the claim.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect)**: A page loading successfully does not establish that it contains the cited figure.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Directly checking the source content and its date is the recommended verification.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect)**: A reputable source does not guarantee that AI reproduced its information accurately. Reputation cannot replace reading the source.

**References**: [ChatGPT search](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/9237897-chatgpt-search)

questions.title: Deciding whether to submit sensitive material to AI
questions.prompt: HR is organizing employee interview records containing names and health information. Put the steps in order so that the output of each step becomes the input to the next.

items.text: Submit the approved copy to AI and have a person review the result.
Inspect the records and list personal or confidential fields, including names and health information.
Check whether the information remaining in the redacted copy is permitted input for the company-approved tool and plan.
Remove or pseudonymize unnecessary fields from the inventory to create a copy.

questions.explanation:
The appropriate sequence is to inventory sensitive information, create a filtered copy, check whether that copy is permitted, and then submit it and review the result. Each step depends on the previous step’s output.

| Order | Step | Dependency and rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | (2) Identify personal and confidential fields | Start with the original records. You must know what is present before deciding what to remove. |
| 2 | (4) Remove or pseudonymize unnecessary fields | Use the inventory to create a copy containing only necessary information. |
| 3 | (3) Check whether the copy is eligible for submission | Assess the information remaining in that copy against the approved tool and plan. Consumer and business offerings differ in retention and training defaults, so permitted information may also differ. |
| 4 | (1) Request AI assistance and review the output | Use the approved copy, then have a person review the result. |

If prohibited information remains even after processing, do not delegate the material to AI.

**References**: [Is my data used for model training? (commercial products)](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/7996868-is-my-data-used-for-model-training) · [Is my data used for model training? (consumer plans)](https://privacy.claude.com/en/articles/10023580-is-my-data-used-for-model-training) · [Enterprise privacy at OpenAI](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/)

questions.title: Human review of AI recommendations in high-risk fields
questions.prompt: Hanbit Capital uses Claude to make customer-specific loan eligibility and credit-limit recommendations that are sent directly to customers. A manager is checking Anthropic’s high-risk use requirements. Which operating approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Have a qualified responsible person meaningfully review the recommendation with authority to change it, and disclose AI involvement to the customer.
If predeployment accuracy is sufficiently high, deliver recommendations automatically without review.
Treat clicking an approval button before sending as sufficient review and omit AI disclosure.
Do not use Claude because all financial uses are prohibited.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic’s High-risk Use Case Requirements cover personalized recommendations in areas such as legal matters, medicine, finance, credit, insurance, and employment. They require meaningful review by a qualified person with authority to change the recommendation and accountability for it, together with clear disclosure of AI use to affected people. General information, internal drafts, or analysis that does not constitute a final personalized recommendation is exempt. Here, recommendations about individual customers’ limits are delivered directly to those customers.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It satisfies both meaningful qualified review and disclosure requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect)**: High measured accuracy does not replace the review requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect)**: Ceremonial approval is not meaningful review. Disclosure is a separate requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect)**: Financial use is not categorically banned; it is allowed when applicable conditions are met.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy › High-risk Use Case Requirements](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)

questions.title: Evaluating administrator controls and policy statements
questions.prompt: Mark each statement Yes if it is correct and No if it is incorrect.

items.text: ChatGPT Business workspace administrators can view, export, and delete employee conversations.
Workspace administrators cannot restrict Gmail or Drive grounding sources and can only enable or disable the feature.
Google prohibits deceptively presenting generated output as solely human-created.
OpenAI prohibits personalized legal or medical advice requiring a license without appropriate involvement of a licensed professional.

questions.explanation:
Administrator controls are available, and provider policies impose restrictions on deception and unreviewed professional advice.

1. **Yes**: The enterprise privacy guidance states that ChatGPT Business workspace administrators can view, export, and delete employee conversations.
2. **No**: Workspace administrators can exclude Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Chat from grounding. Their control is not limited to turning the feature on or off.
3. **Yes**: Google prohibits deceptively attributing generated output solely to human creation.
4. **Yes**: OpenAI requires appropriate licensed-professional involvement for personalized advice that requires a license. This is not a blanket prohibition on discussing legal or medical topics.

**References**: [Enterprise privacy at OpenAI](https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy/) · [Generative AI in Google Workspace Privacy Hub](https://knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/generative-ai/generative-ai-in-google-workspace-privacy-hub) · [Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy](https://policies.google.com/terms/generative-ai/use-policy) · [OpenAI Usage policies](https://openai.com/policies/usage-policies/)

questions.title: Checks before publishing an AI draft
questions.prompt: A public relations employee is preparing to send an AI-drafted press release. Facts, numbers, and quotations have already been checked. It includes the names and statements of experts and partner contacts, and some paragraphs resemble another article. Which TWO additional checks should be performed before publication?

options.text: Check that its tone matches ordinary press releases and conclude that it can be published.
Run only a plagiarism check and treat a passing result as completion of the review.
Check the scope of consent for named individuals’ statements and whether nonpublic information is included.
Ask a colleague to check only for typos, then publish it.
Check whether company or media rules require AI disclosure and whether other people’s writing has been copied.

questions.explanation:
Fact checking does not complete the publication review. Consent and private information require separate consideration: Anthropic prohibits invasions of privacy and misuse of personal information. AI-assisted work also requires appropriate permission and attribution; policy restrictions address plagiarism and submission of AI-assisted results without appropriate permission or attribution.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect)**: Appropriate tone does not establish consent or resolve disclosure obligations.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect)**: An overlap or plagiarism checker does not check consent or whether AI disclosure is required.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: A person must check consent and whether nonpublic information has been included.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect)**: Spelling review leaves rights and disclosure issues unresolved.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Checking disclosure requirements and unauthorized copying supports trust and accountability.

**References**: [Anthropic Usage Policy › Do Not Engage in Fraudulent, Abusive, or Predatory Practices](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) · [Anthropic Usage Policy › Privacy and identity](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup)
